source.title: A Tale of Tails: Model Collapse as a Change of Scaling Laws
source.authors: Elvis Dohmatob; Yunzhen Feng; Pu Yang; François Charton; Julia Kempe

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present; no material truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study develops theory and reports experiments showing that synthetic-data generation can change or halt loss scaling, refining the scope of scaling-law claims.
record.gate_note: The paper tests scaling of test error or perplexity with training sample size under clean, synthetic, repeated-generation, and mixed-data conditions. It also reports GCD skill counts, recorded below as findings that do not fit a listed version. It does not test parameter-count or compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, model-size extrapolation, or architecture-shape invariance. Figure-only curves are not assigned numeric values.
record.test_reason: The study argues and shows that sample-size scaling breaks, plateaus or shifts when training data is model-generated. It uses theory on toy models plus neural experiments: Llama2-7B LoRA fine-tuning and GCD transformers trained from scratch. Those neural experiments bear on V5, whether the power-law form holds in other training regimes such as fine-tuning and synthetic or regenerated data. The study does not vary parameters or compute, does not do LM pretraining, and fits no power laws to its neural curves, so it does not test V1–V4, V6 or V7 directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors go further, saying their work 'signals the end of current neural scaling laws' once synthetic data enters training corpora, with test error tapering off because tails are cut or narrowed. They also say clean-data mixing produces grokking-like recovery, AI data can help when real data is scarce, and watermarking and clean data become more important.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than sweeping model parameters, tokens, or compute to test the original scaling-law recipe, the paper studies theoretical and empirical error scaling under tail-cut, tail-narrowed, mixed, and recursively generated data, including fine-tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior varies with synthetic-data generation and composition: tail cutoff, tail narrowing, number of generations, top-p, temperature, and proportion of clean data.

fits_no_version.finding: In non-neural toy models (Hutter memorizer, Hutter++ bigram estimator, associative memory), tail-cut data adds an error floor k^{-(β−1)}. Tail narrowing changes the exponent to (β−1)/β′. n generations shift error roughly by n. Clean/synthetic mixtures give a plateau of length ~k^β/π before the clean law resumes. Simulations of these estimators match the theory.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under heavy-tailed (Zipf) data, theoretical sample-size scaling laws acquire floors, shifted curves or altered exponents when training data is tail-truncated or narrowed by generation.

fits_no_version.finding: GCD models trained on AI-generated labels add no new correctly predicted GCDs between 300M and 1B examples, while correct-label models do.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training on generated labels can stall skill acquisition that continued clean training achieves.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 235, 2024
record.problems: Much of the theory uses simplified Hutter, bigram, or associative-memory models rather than full language-model pretraining. The Llama2 evidence is a fine-tuning experiment on one 7B model, not a model-size or compute sweep. Many empirical values appear only in plots; numerical loss values and uncertainty estimates are generally not reported for those curves.
record.rows_left_out: The paper includes additional Hutter, Hutter++, bigram, GCD, and Llama plots, including multiple separate generation curves, mixture settings, and appendix figures. The retained plot rows summarize the main prose-described scaling outcomes by setting; per-generation curve coordinates and further plot-only repetitions are not separately extracted.

untested.parts: No LM pretraining; no scaling in parameters, tokens of real pretraining data, or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No shape comparison. The encoder-only vs encoder-decoder GCD remark is anecdotal.
Image/video modalities, transfer, and repeated (as opposed to regenerated) data are not tested. Neural evidence comes from one 7B LoRA fine-tune and small GCD transformers, with no fitted exponents.
No downstream-vs-loss predictability. GCD skill counts are task accuracy, not tied to a loss law.
No comparison of fitting choices. Exponent dependence on data tail appears only in toy theory.

missing.what: GCD mixture (grokking) results: samples until mixture models learn an 'unlearnable' GCD, and delay, by mixture rate (0/9/27/50/73% AI). Delay grows with AI fraction; 73% AI never succeeds within the budget.
Early-training reversal: below about 100M examples, AI-data GCD models predict as many or more correct GCDs than clean models.
Llama2 variants: loss on full chunks including prompt, and a 90/10 generated/original mixture from gen 1.
GCD single-generation scaling curve used in the main text.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The neural evidence is fine-tuning (Llama2-7B LoRA) and arithmetic transformers trained on sample size only; the paper notes it did not train an LLM from scratch. All neural scaling curves are figure-only with no fitted exponents or uncertainties. The theory rows concern non-neural estimators, so they are moved to fits_no_version rather than linked to V1/V5. The study's results on the original law are indirect: they concern data-quality regimes, not the parameter, token or compute laws.

versions.untested_parts: Tests error or perplexity against training sample size in simplified models and selected fine-tuning experiments. Does not test parameter-count or compute scaling, or independently establish that other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No experiment fits laws on small runs and tests predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests synthetic and repeated data, including Llama fine-tuning and arithmetic-task models. Does not test image/video modalities, transfer, or fine-tuning in a systematic range of models and regimes.
Reports task-specific GCD skill learning, but does not test downstream-task performance as a predictable function of pretraining loss or scale.
Does not compare fitting choices or show that published exponents or compute-optimal allocations differ because of such choices.

rows.subject: Hutter LLM (theoretical model)
rows.operation_detail: Derives clean-data test-error scaling with sample size
rows.note: The paper presents this as the usual clean-data scaling law for its simplified model.
rows.check: Eq. 8 is Hutter (2021)'s known clean-data result, which the paper cites. It is a cited result, not a finding of this study, and the system is a non-neural memorizer rather than a language model.

rows.subject: Hutter LLM (theoretical model)
rows.operation_detail: Derives test-error scaling when training data has its tail cut off

conditions.value: AI-generated distribution with cutoff rank k

rows.note: As training size grows past the cutoff-dependent scale, the error plateaus rather than continuing the clean-data decay.
rows.check: Theorem in a non-neural Hutter memorizer, not an LM or a neural model. Better recorded as a theoretical argument under fits_no_version than as a V1/V5 result.

rows.subject: Hutter LLM (theoretical model)
rows.operation_detail: Derives test-error scaling for a narrowed heavy tail

conditions.value: AI-generated long-tail distribution with exponent β′ ∈ (1, β)

rows.note: The decay remains a power law but has a different, slower exponent.
rows.check: Toy-model theorem. It says the exponent changes with the data tail: an argument close to V7, but not about fitted LM laws.

rows.subject: Hutter LLM (theoretical model)
rows.operation_detail: Derives error after recursive generations of synthetic data
rows.note: The per-generation contribution increases the error and shifts the scaling curve.
rows.check: Toy-model theory (Eqs. 12–13), not a measured neural-model result.

rows.subject: Hutter LLM (theoretical model)
rows.operation_detail: Derives scaling for a mixture of clean and tail-cut data

conditions.value: proportion π from true distribution, remainder tail-cut at k

rows.value: Early: Etest ≍ T^{-(1−1/β)} + k^{-(β−1)}; later: Etest ≍ (πT)^{-(1−1/β)}
rows.note: The curve has a plateau before recovering the clean-data sample-size law, with a mixture-dependent cost.
rows.check: Toy-model theory (Theorem 3.2).

rows.subject: Hutter++ (theoretical bigram model)
rows.operation_detail: Derives clean-data error scaling for probabilistic outputs
rows.value: Etest ≲ T^{-c}; under the stated permutation and summability conditions, Etest ≍ T^{-c}, with c = min(1−1/β, 1/2)
rows.note: The theorem states that the clean-data sample-size scaling law is retained in this model.
rows.check: Hutter++ is a count-based bigram estimator, not a neural LM. The clean-data theorem is not evidence on LM pretraining loss.

rows.subject: Hutter++ (theoretical bigram model)
rows.operation_detail: Derives error scaling with a cutoff in the conditional output distribution
rows.note: The cutoff adds an error floor to the clean-data scaling.
rows.check: Toy-model theorem.

rows.subject: Hutter++ empirical bigram model

rows.note: The text describes a notable loss of data scalability for Gen 1 and rapid performance decline across generations.
rows.check: Simulation of a count-based Hutter++ estimator, not a trained neural model.

relationships.condition: Clean-data training: Llama2-7B LoRA fine-tuning on Wikitext-103, and GCD transformers on correct labels
relationships.reason: Clean fine-tuning shows a scaling decay of perplexity with sample size (r13), and clean GCD models keep lowering test loss (r18, r20, r22). Both are figure-only with no exponent fitted.
relationships.display_finding: Clean Llama2-7B fine-tuning perplexity decreased with sample size, while clean-label GCD transformers continued reducing test loss.

source_check.reason: The paper identifies scaling-law decay for clean fine-tuning and continued scaling for clean GCD training (r13, r18, r20, r22); evidence is qualitative, without fitted neural exponents.

relationships.condition: GCD transformers trained only on model-generated labels
relationships.reason: Test loss stops decreasing after about 300M samples while clean models keep improving (r17, r19, r21; Figs 28–29).
relationships.display_finding: Test loss stopped decreasing after about 300M samples, while models trained on clean labels kept improving.

source_check.reason: Appendix G explicitly states that generated-label models stop learning after about 300M examples while clean models continue improving (r17, r19, r21).

relationships.condition: Llama2-7B fine-tuned on recursively generated text, alone or mixed 98/2 with original data
relationships.reason: Generated-data curves keep some but much reduced scaling, weaker at gen 2 (r14, r15). A 2% clean mixture yields a plateau-then-decline curve (r16). All figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Scaling weakened further at generation 2, while adding 2% clean data produced a plateau followed by decline.

reader_labels.reason: The theory adds an error floor or generation-dependent degradation rather than maintaining the clean-data sample-size curve (r2, r4, r7); reported experiments also show tapered scaling or collapse (r8–r15, r17, r19, r21).

reader_labels.reason: The paper reports cutoff-dependent plateaus and degradation across generations; Llama2 generation curves and arithmetic-model losses also taper or stop improving (r2, r4, r7–r15, r17, r19, r21).
